A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the hardware performance of Round 2 candidates is quite diverse, and it is possible to achieve a significant performance boost by implementing at least the major operations of a given algorithm in hardware.

(1) for lattice-based schemes, hardware implementation can be a very effective way to speed up the algorithms, and (2) for all schemes, software-hardware co-designed implementations provide the most efficient solution.

we have demonstrated that hardware implementations are a very useful tool in the NIST PQ Crypto standardization process, and they can provide a significant contribution to the selection of the final PQC standard.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the performance of Round 2 lattice-based PQC candidates, when implemented using FGPAs or ASICs, is comparable to that of the Round 1 candidates, and that the performance gap between the Round 1 winners and the Round 2 lattice candidates is not large.

, in the context of PQC standardization, hardware performance of the best-performing Round 2 candidates is comparable to the best-performing software implementations, and that hardware co-design may be a very useful tool in identifying candidates that may not be suitable for hardware implementations.
, for the most part, the performance of Round 2 candidates is not significantly better than that of their Round 1 counterparts.
